name: writing a software requirements specification
from: Requirement-shaped sentences scattered across designs, conversations, and heads — compound, sourceless, unverifiable — while the SAS answers to a baseline that does not exist and every design element traces into air.
to: A requirements baseline per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148: every requirement singular, unambiguous, and verifiable, carrying the citation that forced it or the ruling that chose it, an allocation, and a trace — with derived requirements distinguished from stakeholder requirements by what forces them, because the two carry different assurance.
cost: The tedium of splitting every compound, sourcing every statement, and sending every unverifiable wish back to its owner for a measure — precision paid one requirement at a time, before any of it feels urgent.
otherwise: The design set answers to nothing checkable, chosen constraints masquerade as forced ones and mint assurance the mathematics never issued, and 'the system meets its requirements' remains a sentence nobody can falsify.
